title: Optics
subject: Physics

cards.prompt: What is Light? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Light is electromagnetic radiation, with visible light occupying only one part of the electromagnetic spectrum. Wave and photon descriptions address different aspects of optical phenomena rather than implying that all optics is visible to the eye.
required_concepts: Electromagnetic radiation broader than the visible band.
major_error_concepts: Assuming nonvisible radiation cannot show reflection, refraction, or interference.

cards.prompt: What is Refractive Index? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Refractive index n is the ratio of vacuum light speed to the phase speed in a material at a stated frequency. It can depend on frequency, direction, or polarization in more general materials.
required_concepts: n=c/v_phase with frequency and medium specified.
major_error_concepts: Using group speed in the definition without distinguishing group index.

cards.prompt: What is Optical Path Length? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Optical path length is the integral of refractive index along a physical path. It determines accumulated phase for a fixed vacuum wavelength in the usual scalar propagation description, and differs from geometric distance alone.
required_concepts: Integral n ds, not only geometric length.
major_error_concepts: Comparing phase through different materials using distance alone while ignoring refractive index.

cards.prompt: What is Geometrical Optics? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A ray is a geometrical-optics representation of propagation direction in a regime where wavelength is small relative to relevant spatial variations. Rays do not describe every diffraction or interference effect by themselves.
required_concepts: Short-wavelength propagation approximation.
major_error_concepts: Treating rays as literal thin material threads that fully describe every optical phenomenon.

cards.prompt: What is Wavefront? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A wavefront is a surface of equal optical phase. In a simple isotropic medium, rays are locally normal to wavefronts, while anisotropic media require distinguishing phase normals from energy-flow direction.
required_concepts: Equal-phase surface.
Ray-normal relation assumes suitable isotropy.
major_error_concepts: Defining a wavefront as a surface of equal intensity regardless of phase.

cards.prompt: What is Fermat Principle? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Fermat's principle states that the physical geometrical-optics path makes optical travel time stationary under suitable nearby path variations. Stationary need not mean the globally shortest geometric path or a strict minimum in every configuration.
required_concepts: Stationary optical travel time.
Not universally minimum geometric distance.
major_error_concepts: Claiming light always follows the shortest physical distance regardless of refractive index.

cards.prompt: What is Reflection Law? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Specular reflection at a smooth interface has equal incident and reflected angles measured from the local normal, with incident ray, reflected ray, and normal coplanar. Angle conventions must use the normal rather than the surface tangent.
required_concepts: Equal normal-referenced angles and coplanar rays.
major_error_concepts: Measuring one angle from the normal and the other from the surface while asserting equality.

cards.prompt: What is Specular and Diffuse Reflection? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Specular reflection preserves a definite direction from a smooth surface at the relevant wavelength scale. Diffuse reflection distributes light across directions because of surface structure or scattering; it does not contradict local electromagnetic reflection laws.
required_concepts: Directional smooth-surface reflection versus angularly spread reflection.
major_error_concepts: Claiming diffuse reflection means no physical reflection law applies locally.

cards.prompt: What is Snell Law? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Snell's law is n_1 sin theta_1=n_2 sin theta_2 at a stationary isotropic interface, with angles measured from the normal. Refraction depends on the indices at the light's frequency.
required_concepts: Index-weighted sine-angle equality.
major_error_concepts: Using angles measured from the surface in the normal-angle formula without conversion.

cards.term: Frequency and Wavelength at an Interface
cards.prompt: What is Frequency and Wavelength at an Interface? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: At a stationary linear interface, transmitted and reflected waves share the incident frequency. Wavelength changes when phase speed changes, following lambda_medium=lambda_vacuum/n for a simple medium.
required_concepts: Frequency retained and wavelength adjusted by index.
major_error_concepts: Assuming light changes frequency solely because it enters a stationary transparent medium.

cards.prompt: What is Optical Dispersion? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Optical dispersion is the frequency dependence of a medium's propagation response, often represented by n(omega). It can separate colors in a prism and make phase and group velocities differ.
required_concepts: Frequency-dependent refractive behavior.
major_error_concepts: Equating dispersion with absorption or assuming all frequencies have one universal index.

cards.prompt: What is Total Internal Reflection? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Total internal reflection occurs for incidence from a higher-index to a lower-index transparent medium above the critical angle in the ideal lossless interface model. It can coexist with an evanescent field on the lower-index side.
required_concepts: High-to-low index and above-critical incidence.
major_error_concepts: Claiming total internal reflection occurs for any low-to-high index incidence angle.

cards.prompt: What is Critical Angle? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: For n_1 greater than n_2, the critical angle satisfies sin theta_c=n_2/n_1. At this limiting angle the transmitted propagating ray is tangent to the interface in the ideal ray description.
required_concepts: Critical angle from lower-to-higher index ratio.
accepted_variants: Threshold angle for total internal reflection.
major_error_concepts: Using n_1/n_2 inside arcsine for high-to-low incidence.

cards.prompt: What is Evanescent Field? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: An evanescent field decays exponentially in a spatial direction instead of propagating with an ordinary real wavenumber in that direction. Near a total-internal-reflection interface it can exist beyond the boundary and couple to nearby structures.
required_concepts: Exponential spatial decay and near-boundary existence.
major_error_concepts: Assuming total internal reflection means the electromagnetic field is identically zero just beyond the interface.

cards.prompt: What is Optical Fiber? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: An optical fiber guides light through a refractive-index structure, commonly a higher-index core surrounded by lower-index cladding. Ray total internal reflection gives intuition, while actual guided modes and cutoff require wave analysis.
required_concepts: Index-guided propagation with modal description beyond rays.
major_error_concepts: Assuming every ray entering a fiber must be guided regardless of angle, wavelength, or core size.

cards.prompt: What is Plane Mirror Image? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A plane mirror forms a virtual image the same perpendicular distance behind the mirror as the object is in front, for the standard uniform-medium geometry. The image is upright with unit transverse magnification.
required_concepts: Virtual symmetric image position and unit size.
major_error_concepts: Claiming rays physically converge behind an ordinary plane mirror.

cards.prompt: What is Spherical Mirror? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A spherical mirror uses a surface with a spherical curvature radius. In the paraxial approximation its focal length magnitude is half the radius, with convergence or divergence determined by whether the reflecting surface is concave or convex.
required_concepts: Paraxial spherical-mirror focal length magnitude R/2.
major_error_concepts: Assuming rays arbitrarily far from the axis share an exact common spherical-mirror focus.

cards.prompt: What is Mirror Equation? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Using a real-positive mirror convention, paraxial imaging obeys 1/f=1/s_o+1/s_i, with real object and image distances positive and a converging mirror's f positive. A sign convention must be used consistently rather than mixed across diagrams.
required_concepts: Paraxial mirror imaging equation with explicit consistent signs.
major_error_concepts: Combining a signed focal length from one convention with distances from an incompatible convention.

cards.prompt: What is Mirror Magnification? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: In the stated real-positive paraxial mirror convention, transverse magnification is m=-s_i/s_o. Its magnitude gives size ratio and its sign indicates inversion relative to the chosen transverse coordinate orientation.
required_concepts: Magnification minus image distance over object distance.
major_error_concepts: Treating negative magnification as a negative physical object size rather than orientation reversal.

cards.prompt: What is Paraxial Approximation? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: The paraxial approximation restricts rays to small angles near an optical axis, allowing sin theta and tan theta to be approximated by theta in radians. It underlies simple first-order lens and mirror formulas and omits higher-order aberrations.
required_concepts: Small-angle near-axis approximation.
major_error_concepts: Using degree values directly in sin theta approximately theta without conversion to radians.

cards.prompt: What is Thin Lens? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A thin lens is modeled as changing ray direction at one plane while its thickness is negligible relative to relevant imaging distances. It can converge or diverge rays depending on surface shapes and index contrast, not shape alone in every medium.
required_concepts: Negligible-thickness refraction model.
major_error_concepts: Assuming any visually convex lens converges light regardless of the surrounding medium's index.

cards.prompt: What is Focal Length? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A lens's focal point is the paraxial convergence point of incident parallel rays, or the point from which their outgoing extensions appear to diverge. Focal length is measured using the model's appropriate plane or principal plane.
required_concepts: Parallel-ray focus or virtual origin.
Reference plane matters.
major_error_concepts: Equating focal length with the image distance for every finite object distance.

cards.prompt: What is Thin-Lens Equation? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: For a thin lens using real-positive distances, 1/f=1/s_o+1/s_i, with positive f for a converging lens and negative image distance for a virtual image. The equation assumes paraxial imaging and the adopted common-medium model.
required_concepts: Thin-lens reciprocal distance relation with signed convention.
major_error_concepts: Applying the paraxial equation unchanged to arbitrary thick, strongly off-axis imaging.

cards.prompt: What is Lens Magnification? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: For an ideal thin lens in the stated real-positive convention, transverse magnification is m=-s_i/s_o. It relates image height to object height and differs from angular magnification of an instrument viewed by an eye.
required_concepts: Image-to-object height ratio from signed distances.
major_error_concepts: Equating transverse magnification with every telescope's angular magnification.

cards.prompt: What is Real and Virtual Images? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A real image forms where outgoing rays physically converge and can be intercepted by a screen in the ideal geometry. A virtual image is located where backward extensions of outgoing rays intersect, without actual convergence there.
required_concepts: Actual convergence versus apparent intersection of extensions.
major_error_concepts: Assuming a virtual image cannot be seen because it cannot be projected directly onto a screen at its apparent location.

cards.prompt: What is Ray Construction? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A paraxial ray construction locates an image by tracing a small set of rays whose behavior is known, such as parallel, focal, and central rays for a thin lens. Their intersection represents the same model as the lens equation, not an independent exact treatment of aberrations.
required_concepts: Use known paraxial rays to locate the image.
major_error_concepts: Treating the thin-lens central-ray rule as exact for every thick optical system.

cards.prompt: What is Optical Power? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Optical power is the reciprocal of focal length in meters, measured in inverse meters or diopters under the standard common-medium lens convention. A converging thin lens has positive power and a diverging one negative power.
required_concepts: Power=1/f with f in meters.
major_error_concepts: Using focal length in centimeters without converting while reporting diopters.

cards.prompt: What is Lenses in Contact? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: For thin lenses in contact in the same surrounding medium, equivalent powers add. Separating the lenses changes the combination and generally requires accounting for propagation between them.
required_concepts: Contact thin-lens powers add under common-medium assumptions.
major_error_concepts: Applying contact addition unchanged to lenses separated by a substantial distance.

cards.prompt: What is Separated Lenses? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Separated lens systems are analyzed by propagation between elements, using an intermediate image as the next element's object with consistent signs. The equivalent focal behavior depends on both powers and separation.
required_concepts: Sequential imaging with propagation and signed intermediate objects.
major_error_concepts: Ignoring separation when computing the effective behavior of two distant lenses.

cards.prompt: What is Ray-Transfer Matrix? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: An ABCD ray matrix maps paraxial ray height and angle between reference planes using a stated coordinate convention. Matrix multiplication composes elements in traversal order, and index changes affect which determinant or invariant statements apply.
required_concepts: Linear map of paraxial ray coordinates.
Conventions and composition order matter.
major_error_concepts: Multiplying optical elements in arbitrary order because matrix multiplication is assumed commutative.

cards.prompt: What is Principal Planes? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Principal planes are reference planes that let a centered optical system's paraxial imaging be represented by equivalent focal properties. They need not coincide with a physical glass surface or even lie inside the system.
required_concepts: Equivalent-system paraxial reference planes.
major_error_concepts: Measuring every thick-system focal distance from the nearest physical surface regardless of principal-plane location.

cards.prompt: What is Optical Axis? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: The optical axis is the reference line associated with the symmetry or alignment of a centered optical system. Off-axis ray behavior and field position are measured relative to it; misaligned systems need a more general description.
required_concepts: Reference symmetry or alignment line.
major_error_concepts: Assuming every arbitrary misaligned collection of lenses has one exact common symmetry axis.

cards.prompt: What is Aperture Stop? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: The aperture stop is the element that limits the axial cone of admitted rays in a given optical system. It need not be the first opening or the smallest physical hole when preceding optics change apparent aperture sizes.
required_concepts: Element limiting the admitted axial ray cone.
major_error_concepts: Identifying the aperture stop solely by the smallest measured hole without considering optical imaging.

cards.prompt: What is Optical Pupils? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: The entrance pupil is the image of the aperture stop seen through optics before it, while the exit pupil is its image through optics after it. Pupil size and location can differ from the physical stop.
required_concepts: Stop images through preceding and following optics.
major_error_concepts: Equating every pupil directly with the physical stop regardless of intervening lenses.

cards.prompt: What is F-Number? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: For a common camera-like system, f-number is focal length divided by entrance-pupil diameter. A smaller f-number admits a wider cone for a fixed focal length, but transmission losses are separate from this geometric ratio.
required_concepts: f-number=f/entrance-pupil diameter.
major_error_concepts: Using an arbitrary barrel diameter rather than the entrance pupil when calculating f-number.

cards.prompt: What is Numerical Aperture? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Numerical aperture is n sin theta for the accepted or emitted cone half-angle in a specified medium. It describes angular light collection and is important for resolution, with object-side and image-side definitions kept distinct.
required_concepts: Index-weighted sine of cone half-angle.
major_error_concepts: Reporting an NA without identifying the relevant medium and cone when those distinctions matter.

cards.prompt: What is Depth of Field? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Depth of field is the range of object distances judged acceptably sharp for a specified image criterion and system setting. It depends on aperture, magnification, focus distance, and the acceptable blur definition, not an absolute sharpness boundary.
required_concepts: Acceptable object-distance sharpness range.
Blur criterion and settings matter.
major_error_concepts: Treating depth of field as an exact universal range independent of image-size or blur criterion.

cards.prompt: What is Depth of Focus? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Depth of focus is the tolerated displacement of the image plane while meeting a specified blur criterion. It is an image-side quantity and differs from the object-distance range called depth of field.
required_concepts: Image-plane positional tolerance.
major_error_concepts: Using depth of field and depth of focus as identical object-side quantities.

cards.prompt: What is Spherical Aberration? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Spherical aberration makes rays from different aperture zones focus at different axial positions in an imperfect imaging system. It can occur even for on-axis monochromatic light and is omitted by ideal first-order paraxial imaging.
required_concepts: Aperture-dependent focus for on-axis rays.
major_error_concepts: Defining spherical aberration solely as a color-dependent focal shift.

cards.prompt: What is Chromatic Aberration? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Chromatic aberration is color-dependent imaging caused by dispersion, such as different focal locations or magnifications at different wavelengths. Combining appropriate optical elements can reduce selected chromatic errors without eliminating every aberration.
required_concepts: Dispersion causes wavelength-dependent imaging.
major_error_concepts: Assuming a lens has one exactly common focus for all wavelengths merely because it is paraxial.

cards.prompt: What is Coma? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Coma is an off-axis aberration in which rays from different pupil regions produce an asymmetric comet-like point image. It differs from uniform image displacement or a purely on-axis spherical blur.
required_concepts: Asymmetric off-axis point-image blur.
major_error_concepts: Calling any symmetric defocus spot coma.

cards.prompt: What is Optical Astigmatism? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Off-axis astigmatism produces different focusing behavior in two principal ray-plane sections, commonly yielding separate tangential and sagittal foci. It differs from a single common focus simply shifted along the axis.
required_concepts: Different focal behavior in principal off-axis sections.
major_error_concepts: Equating all astigmatism with simple uniform defocus at one focal plane.

cards.prompt: What is Image Distortion? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Distortion changes image magnification with field position so shapes are warped, such as barrel or pincushion patterns. It can occur while individual point images remain relatively sharp, unlike aberrations defined primarily by blur.
required_concepts: Field-dependent magnification warps geometry.
major_error_concepts: Assuming distortion necessarily means every point is out of focus.

cards.prompt: What is Aberration and Diffraction? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Aberration comes from departures of an optical system's wavefront or ray mapping from ideal imaging, while diffraction arises from wave propagation through finite apertures. Removing aberrations does not remove the finite-aperture diffraction limit.
required_concepts: Distinguish imperfect imaging from finite-aperture wave spreading.
major_error_concepts: Claiming a perfectly corrected finite lens forms an infinitely small point image.

cards.prompt: What is Eye Optics? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: In a simplified eye model, the cornea and lens focus incoming light onto the retina, which detects the image. This optical model describes image formation rather than establishing the full neural process of visual perception.
required_concepts: Refractive focusing onto a detector surface.
major_error_concepts: Equating the retinal optical image alone with every aspect of visual perception.

cards.prompt: What is Accommodation? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Accommodation changes the eye's effective optical power to focus on different object distances. In the standard simplified model this occurs mainly through changes in crystalline-lens shape rather than moving the retina back and forth.
required_concepts: Variable lens power changes focus distance.
major_error_concepts: Assuming accommodation works primarily by changing the eye's detector position arbitrarily.

cards.prompt: What is Myopia as an Optical Model? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: In the simplified optical description of myopia, parallel incident rays focus in front of the retina when accommodation is relaxed. A diverging correction can shift the effective focus backward in that model; individual diagnosis is outside this concept definition.
required_concepts: Relaxed distant focus lies before retina in the model.
major_error_concepts: Describing myopia as distant parallel rays focusing behind the retina in the basic model.

cards.prompt: What is Hyperopia as an Optical Model? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: In the simplified optical description of hyperopia, relaxed distant focusing would occur behind the retina, and converging correction can help bring the focus forward. Accommodation and individual anatomy affect actual focusing, so this is an optical model rather than a clinical prescription.
required_concepts: Relaxed distant focus behind retina in the model.
major_error_concepts: Equating hyperopia with every age-related loss of accommodation.

cards.prompt: What is Simple Magnifier? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A simple magnifier increases the angular size of a nearby object by forming an enlarged virtual image under suitable placement. Its useful magnification depends on viewing geometry and the chosen reference unaided viewing distance.
required_concepts: Angular enlargement through a virtual image.
major_error_concepts: Claiming angular magnification is always the same as image-height divided by object-height without specifying viewing geometry.

cards.prompt: What is Compound Microscope? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A compound microscope uses an objective to form an intermediate image and an eyepiece or detector optics to present it for viewing or recording. Resolution is limited by wavelength and numerical aperture as well as aberrations, not only nominal magnification.
required_concepts: Objective image followed by viewing or detection optics.
Magnification alone does not ensure resolution.
major_error_concepts: Assuming arbitrarily high magnification creates new detail beyond the optical resolution limit.

cards.prompt: What is Telescope? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: An astronomical telescope collects light from distant objects and changes their apparent angular size. In an ideal afocal two-positive-lens model, angular magnification has magnitude f_objective/f_eyepiece, with image orientation determined by the configuration.
required_concepts: Distant-object angular imaging.
Focal-length ratio for the stated ideal arrangement.
major_error_concepts: Using transverse image magnification as the telescope's angular magnification without a viewing model.

cards.prompt: What is Camera Imaging? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A camera forms a real image on a detector using its lens system. Aperture, exposure time, focus, sensor response, and scene illumination jointly affect the recorded image; focal length alone does not determine exposure or sharpness.
required_concepts: Real-image recording with multiple optical and acquisition controls.
major_error_concepts: Assuming equal focal lengths guarantee equal collected light regardless of aperture or exposure.

cards.prompt: What is Radiometry and Photometry? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Radiometry measures optical energy and power using physical energy-based quantities. It differs from photometry, which weights visible light by a specified human visual-response function.
required_concepts: Energy-based optical measurement versus visual-response weighting.
major_error_concepts: Treating equal radiant power at all wavelengths as equal perceived brightness by definition.

cards.prompt: What is Irradiance? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Irradiance is radiant power incident per unit area of a receiving surface, including the effect of incidence geometry. It differs from total power and from radiance resolved by direction.
required_concepts: Incident power per receiving area.
major_error_concepts: Reporting total watts as irradiance without specifying receiving area.

cards.prompt: What is Radiance? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Radiance describes radiant power per projected source area per solid angle in a specified direction. It retains both spatial and angular information, unlike irradiance which integrates incoming directions at a receiving surface.
required_concepts: Power per projected area per solid angle.
accepted_variants: Directional optical brightness in radiometric units.
major_error_concepts: Equating radiance with total power per detector area after angular integration.

cards.prompt: What is Brightness Conservation? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: In ideal passive lossless geometrical optics, radiance divided by refractive index squared is conserved along appropriate rays. Concentration trades area against angular spread and cannot freely increase source brightness under those assumptions.
required_concepts: Radiance-index invariant in passive lossless ray optics.
Area-angular tradeoff.
major_error_concepts: Assuming passive lenses can increase radiance without limit merely by focusing to a smaller area.

cards.prompt: What is Optical Coherence? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Optical coherence describes phase correlations across time or positions that support reproducible interference. Two beams with equal central wavelength are not necessarily mutually coherent over the observation interval.
required_concepts: Phase correlation, not wavelength equality alone.
major_error_concepts: Assuming any independent same-color light sources produce stable fringes automatically.

cards.prompt: What is Optical Phase? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Optical phase specifies position within a field oscillation and accumulates through optical path length. Only a phase difference relative to another field or reference affects an ordinary interference comparison.
required_concepts: Oscillation phase and relative-phase measurement.
major_error_concepts: Treating an arbitrary global phase offset as changing a single beam's time-averaged intensity.

cards.prompt: What is Optical Interference? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Interference results from adding coherent optical fields before computing intensity. The cross term depends on relative phase, amplitude, polarization, and coherence, so intensity addition alone is insufficient in the coherent case.
required_concepts: Field addition precedes intensity.
Cross term depends on phase and compatibility.
major_error_concepts: Adding coherent beam intensities while ignoring the field cross term.

cards.prompt: What is Two-Beam Interference? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: For two fully coherent same-polarization beams, intensity is I_1+I_2+2sqrt(I_1 I_2)cos delta under consistent normalization. Incoherence or orthogonal polarizations can suppress the measured cross term.
required_concepts: Two-beam cross term and assumptions.
major_error_concepts: Applying the full cross term unchanged to orthogonally polarized beams without an analyzer or coupling.

cards.prompt: What is Fringe Visibility? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Fringe visibility is (I_max-I_min)/(I_max+I_min) for a nonzero summed intensity. It reflects contrast and depends on coherence, intensity balance, polarization, and instrumental averaging rather than coherence alone.
required_concepts: Normalized max-min fringe contrast.
major_error_concepts: Treating low visibility as proof of low coherence without considering unequal intensities or polarization.

cards.prompt: What is Young Double-Slit Experiment? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Young's double-slit arrangement produces interference from two coherent apertures, with phase difference set by their path difference to the screen. Finite slit width adds a diffraction envelope over the two-slit fringes.
required_concepts: Two coherent apertures create path-dependent interference.
Finite widths add an envelope.
major_error_concepts: Assuming every bright fringe has equal intensity regardless of the slit diffraction pattern.

cards.prompt: What is Double-Slit Fringe Spacing? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: For slit separation d, wavelength lambda, and a distant screen at distance L in the small-angle regime, Young-fringe spacing is approximately lambda L/d. The wavelength must refer to the propagation medium used in the geometry.
required_concepts: Small-angle fringe spacing lambda L/d.
major_error_concepts: Using the approximation unchanged at large angles or near-screen geometry without correction.

cards.prompt: What is Thin-Film Interference? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Thin-film interference combines beams reflected or transmitted at a film's interfaces. Relative phase includes propagation through the film and any interface phase shifts, so constructive conditions cannot be inferred from thickness alone.
required_concepts: Film propagation phase plus interface phase changes.
major_error_concepts: Applying a path-length rule while ignoring a reflection phase reversal.

cards.prompt: What is Reflection Phase Shift? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: At normal incidence between simple transparent nonmagnetic dielectrics, electric-field reflection from lower to higher index introduces a pi phase reversal under a consistent transverse-field convention. Higher-to-lower reflection has no such reversal in that normal-incidence model.
required_concepts: Normal-incidence reflection phase depends on index direction.
major_error_concepts: Applying the simple normal-incidence rule unchanged to every polarization and total-internal-reflection angle.

cards.prompt: What is Optical Wedge Fringes? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A wedge-shaped thin film changes thickness across position, producing spatial fringes from varying optical path difference. Fringe spacing depends on wavelength, wedge geometry, index, and the chosen reflection or transmission arrangement.
required_concepts: Thickness gradient creates spatial phase gradient.
major_error_concepts: Treating wedge fringes as independent of film thickness variation.

cards.prompt: What is Michelson Interferometer? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A Michelson interferometer splits light into two arms and recombines their returned beams. Moving one end mirror by delta x changes the round-trip geometric path by 2 delta x in the simple normal-incidence air-arm model.
required_concepts: Split-return-recombine arms.
Mirror displacement doubles the path change.
major_error_concepts: Counting a moved mirror's path change only once despite the outbound and return traversal.

cards.prompt: What is Mach-Zehnder Interferometer? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A Mach-Zehnder interferometer uses two beam splitters and separate paths to split and recombine beams without the Michelson retracing geometry. Relative arm phase redistributes output intensities, with both output ports included in energy accounting.
required_concepts: Separate-path splitting and recombination.
Relative phase controls outputs.
major_error_concepts: Claiming darkening one lossless output port means the total input energy is destroyed.

cards.prompt: What is Fabry-Perot Interferometer? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A Fabry-Perot interferometer uses repeated reflections between two surfaces to form multiple-beam interference. Resonant transmission occurs when round-trip phase is compatible with constructive buildup, including interface phase contributions.
required_concepts: Multiple round trips produce narrow phase-selective resonances.
major_error_concepts: Modeling every Fabry-Perot fringe as only one pair of reflections when repeated amplitudes are important.

cards.prompt: What is Optical Finesse? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Finesse is a resonator's free spectral range divided by a specified resonance linewidth, commonly full width at half maximum. It describes separation of neighboring resonances relative to width and differs from quality factor, which uses the resonance frequency itself.
required_concepts: FSR divided by resonance linewidth.
major_error_concepts: Equating finesse with resonance frequency divided by linewidth without recognizing that expression as quality factor.

cards.prompt: What is Coherence Length? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Coherence length is a characteristic optical path difference over which phase correlations remain sufficient for the specified interference criterion. It is related to spectral width, but precise factors depend on spectrum shape and width definitions.
required_concepts: Path-length scale for maintained interference coherence.
major_error_concepts: Assigning an exact universal coherence length from bandwidth without specifying spectral shape or width convention.

cards.prompt: What is Temporal Coherence? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Temporal coherence measures correlation of an optical field with itself at different times. A narrower spectrum usually gives longer coherence time, while a broad spectrum decorrelates more quickly under comparable definitions.
required_concepts: Correlation across time delay with spectral-width connection.
major_error_concepts: Equating temporal coherence with uniform intensity independent of time.

cards.prompt: What is Spatial Coherence? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Spatial coherence measures phase correlation between different positions in a field. Source size, propagation, apertures, and the separation being compared affect it; it is distinct from the field merely having a uniform brightness.
required_concepts: Field correlation across spatial separation.
major_error_concepts: Assuming a uniformly bright extended source is perfectly spatially coherent everywhere.

cards.prompt: What is Mutual Coherence? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A mutual coherence function correlates complex fields at two positions and times or delays. Normalizing it separates correlation strength from the absolute beam intensities, with the measurement convention explicitly stated.
required_concepts: Two-point delayed complex field correlation.
major_error_concepts: Using intensity correlation as though it were the same quantity as first-order field coherence in every case.

cards.prompt: What is Diffraction? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Diffraction is wave spreading and interference caused by propagation with apertures, obstacles, or other spatial constraints. Its importance depends on wavelength and geometry; geometrical rays alone miss the detailed diffraction pattern.
required_concepts: Wave response to spatial boundaries beyond simple rays.
major_error_concepts: Assuming a perfectly manufactured finite aperture cannot diffract light.

cards.prompt: What is Huygens-Fresnel Principle? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: The Huygens-Fresnel description builds a propagated field from coherent secondary contributions across a wavefront or aperture. Their amplitudes, phases, and geometry must be combined, not just their intensities added independently.
required_concepts: Coherent secondary-wave contributions construct propagation.
major_error_concepts: Adding secondary intensities while discarding the phases needed for a diffraction pattern.

cards.prompt: What is Fraunhofer Diffraction? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Fraunhofer diffraction is the far-field diffraction regime, or its lens-generated equivalent, where the field pattern relates to the aperture's Fourier transform under scalar paraxial assumptions. It is an approximation governed by propagation scales and geometry.
required_concepts: Far-field Fourier-pattern approximation.
major_error_concepts: Assuming any observation distance is automatically in the Fraunhofer regime.

cards.prompt: What is Fresnel Diffraction? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Fresnel diffraction describes near-to-intermediate propagation where quadratic phase variation across the aperture must be retained in the usual paraxial approximation. Its pattern generally changes with propagation distance rather than only rescaling a far-field pattern.
required_concepts: Retain quadratic propagation phase.
major_error_concepts: Using the same distance-independent angular pattern for every Fresnel propagation plane.

cards.prompt: What is Fresnel Number? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A Fresnel number is a squared aperture-size scale divided by wavelength times propagation distance, F approximately a squared/(lambda L) with size convention stated. Small values often support a far-field approximation, while larger values indicate important near-field structure.
required_concepts: Dimensionless aperture-squared over wavelength-distance ratio.
major_error_concepts: Using a Fresnel-number threshold without specifying aperture-size convention or the desired approximation accuracy.

cards.prompt: What is Single-Slit Diffraction? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: For a uniformly illuminated slit of width a in the Fraunhofer regime, intensity follows a sinc-squared angular envelope. Noncentral minima satisfy a sin theta=m lambda for nonzero integers m under the usual scalar model.
required_concepts: Single-slit sinc-squared pattern and nonzero-order minima.
major_error_concepts: Taking m=0 as a central diffraction minimum rather than the central maximum.

cards.prompt: What is Diffraction Envelope? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A diffraction envelope modulates the intensity of a finer interference pattern because each finite aperture has its own angular response. Fringe positions and envelope zeros follow different geometric scales.
required_concepts: Finite-aperture response weights interference fringes.
major_error_concepts: Assuming slit separation and slit width determine the same independent angular scale.

cards.prompt: What is Double-Slit Diffraction Pattern? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Two finite identical slits produce a single-slit diffraction envelope multiplied by a two-slit interference factor under uniform coherent illumination. Some interference maxima can be missing when they coincide with envelope zeros.
required_concepts: Envelope times two-slit factor.
Coincident envelope zeros suppress fringes.
major_error_concepts: Adding an envelope intensity to an interference intensity instead of combining the appropriate field-derived factors.

cards.prompt: What is Circular-Aperture Diffraction? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A uniformly illuminated circular aperture produces an Airy diffraction pattern in the far-field scalar model. Its central lobe is surrounded by rings because the aperture transform differs from that of a rectangular slit.
required_concepts: Circular aperture produces Airy pattern.
major_error_concepts: Using the one-dimensional slit sinc-squared pattern as the exact circular-aperture response.

cards.prompt: What is Airy Disk Scale? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: For a circular aperture of diameter D, the first Airy minimum lies at small angle approximately 1.22 lambda/D in the ideal far-field model. This is an angular radius from the center, not the full central-disk diameter.
required_concepts: First minimum angular radius about 1.22lambda/D.
major_error_concepts: Calling 1.22lambda/D the full angular diameter of the Airy disk without doubling.

cards.prompt: What is Rayleigh Resolution? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: The Rayleigh criterion for two equal incoherent point sources places one ideal diffraction peak at the first minimum of the other. It is a conventional resolution criterion, not a universal hard boundary for every source, detector, or inference method.
required_concepts: Peak-to-first-minimum convention for equal incoherent points.
major_error_concepts: Claiming all distinguishability becomes physically impossible below one criterion regardless of measurement assumptions.

cards.prompt: What is Diffraction Grating? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A diffraction grating uses many regularly spaced scattering or transmitting features to produce narrow interference orders. Feature spacing sets principal order directions, while the number and shape of illuminated features affect width and intensity.
required_concepts: Many periodic features create angularly selected orders.
major_error_concepts: Assuming only the number of slits determines order angles regardless of spacing.

cards.prompt: What is Grating Equation? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: For normal incidence on a simple transmission grating of period d in a common medium, principal orders satisfy d sin theta_m=m lambda. Oblique incidence or different media require the corresponding phase-matching relation rather than this special case.
required_concepts: Normal-incidence grating order equation.
accepted_variants: Grating equation in the stated geometry.
major_error_concepts: Applying normal-incidence angles unchanged when the input beam is oblique.

cards.prompt: What is Grating Orders? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A grating order is an integer-labeled direction of constructive phase matching. An order propagates only when the corresponding angular condition is physically allowed; different wavelengths in different orders can overlap.
required_concepts: Integer interference order with propagation constraint.
major_error_concepts: Assuming every arbitrarily large integer order must produce a propagating beam.

cards.prompt: What is Grating Resolving Power? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: An ideal grating illuminated over N coherent equally spaced periods has resolving power lambda/Delta lambda approximately |m|N in order m under the standard criterion. Slit width, aberrations, detector sampling, and illumination can further limit practical resolution.
required_concepts: Ideal grating resolving power scales as order times illuminated period count.
major_error_concepts: Using total manufactured grooves instead of effectively illuminated coherent grooves without checking illumination.

cards.prompt: What is Blazed Grating? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A blazed grating shapes each period to direct more optical power into a chosen order or wavelength range. Blazing redistributes efficiency and does not remove the overall phase-matching grating equation.
required_concepts: Feature shape favors selected order efficiency.
major_error_concepts: Assuming blazing changes the grating period's order-angle relation arbitrarily.

cards.prompt: What is Prism and Grating Dispersion? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A prism separates wavelengths through refractive dispersion, whereas a grating separates them through wavelength-dependent phase matching across periodic features. Their angular dispersion and order-overlap behavior therefore have different mechanisms.
required_concepts: Refraction dispersion versus periodic interference.
major_error_concepts: Attributing grating dispersion solely to the bulk material's refractive-index variation.

cards.prompt: What is Fourier Optics? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Fourier optics analyzes optical fields through spatial-frequency components and their propagation or filtering in linear systems. Its scalar paraxial forms rely on approximations and do not automatically capture every vector or strongly nonparaxial effect.
required_concepts: Spatial-frequency description of linear optical fields.
major_error_concepts: Treating scalar paraxial Fourier optics as exact for every subwavelength vector-field structure.

cards.prompt: What is Aperture Fourier Transform? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: In coherent Fraunhofer diffraction, far-field amplitude is proportional to the aperture field's Fourier transform with appropriate phase and scale factors. Intensity is the squared magnitude of that transformed amplitude, not the transform of aperture intensity in general.
required_concepts: Transform aperture field, then square magnitude.
major_error_concepts: Fourier-transforming intensity directly while claiming the general coherent far-field amplitude.

cards.prompt: What is Spatial Frequency? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Spatial frequency measures how rapidly a pattern or field varies with position, using cycles per length or an explicitly angular convention. High spatial frequencies represent fine variation and can be removed by an imaging system's finite passband.
required_concepts: Pattern variation rate in space.
Cycle and angular conventions differ.
major_error_concepts: Equating spatial frequency with temporal optical frequency without a propagation or imaging relation.

cards.prompt: What is Point-Spread Function? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A point-spread function describes the image response to a point source under specified imaging conditions. For a linear shift-invariant incoherent intensity system, object intensity is convolved with the intensity PSF; coherent field imaging uses a different amplitude response.
required_concepts: Point-source imaging response with coherence convention stated.
major_error_concepts: Using an incoherent intensity convolution unchanged for arbitrary coherent fields.

cards.prompt: What is Optical Transfer Function? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: For a linear shift-invariant incoherent imaging system, the optical transfer function is the Fourier transform of the intensity PSF. It describes how each object-intensity spatial frequency changes in magnitude and phase.
required_concepts: Fourier transform of intensity PSF under incoherent imaging assumptions.
major_error_concepts: Equating the incoherent OTF with the pupil amplitude directly without the appropriate relation.

cards.prompt: What is Modulation Transfer Function? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: The modulation transfer function is the magnitude of the normalized optical transfer function. It measures contrast transfer by spatial frequency but does not retain phase shifts that can also affect image structure.
required_concepts: Magnitude of normalized OTF.
Phase information excluded.
major_error_concepts: Claiming MTF alone describes every phase distortion of an image.

cards.prompt: What is Polarization? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Polarization describes the direction and evolution of a light wave's transverse electric field. Relative amplitudes and phases of transverse components determine linear, circular, or elliptical states in a monochromatic description.
required_concepts: Transverse electric-field oscillation state.
major_error_concepts: Defining polarization as the direction of beam propagation rather than electric-field oscillation.

cards.prompt: What is Linear Polarization? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Linearly polarized light has its electric field oscillating along one fixed transverse line. The signed field reverses every half-cycle, but the polarization axis remains the same unoriented line.
required_concepts: Fixed transverse oscillation axis.
major_error_concepts: Assuming linear polarization means the electric field always points in one signed direction without oscillating.

cards.prompt: What is Circular Polarization? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Circular polarization occurs when two orthogonal transverse components have equal amplitudes and a quarter-cycle phase difference. The electric-field tip rotates on a circle, with handedness defined only after a propagation and viewing convention is specified.
required_concepts: Equal orthogonal amplitudes and quadrature phase.
Handedness convention needed.
major_error_concepts: Claiming equal component amplitudes alone ensure circular polarization regardless of relative phase.

cards.prompt: What is Elliptical Polarization? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Elliptical polarization is the general fixed-frequency fully polarized state whose transverse electric-field tip traces an ellipse. Linear and circular polarization are limiting or special cases set by component amplitudes and phase.
required_concepts: General polarization ellipse.
major_error_concepts: Assuming elliptical polarization requires random field directions rather than a definite phase relation.

cards.prompt: What is Jones Vector? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A Jones vector gives the two complex transverse field amplitudes of fully polarized monochromatic light in a chosen basis. Jones matrices model deterministic linear optical transformations, but ordinary Jones vectors do not alone represent partially polarized mixtures.
required_concepts: Two complex field components in a stated basis.
Fully polarized-state limitation.
major_error_concepts: Representing every unpolarized mixture as one deterministic Jones vector without statistical averaging.

cards.prompt: What is Stokes Parameters? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: For fixed transverse x,y axes, Stokes parameters can be written S0=Ix+Iy (total intensity), S1=Ix-Iy, S2=I45-I135, and S3=IL-IR in the declared left-minus-right circular convention. They describe partially as well as fully polarized light. For a physical beam S1^2+S2^2+S3^2 <= S0^2; an unpolarized beam has S1=S2=S3=0 but may have S0>0. Other circular handedness/sign conventions are valid when defined consistently.
required_concepts: Identify S0 as total intensity, S1 and S2 as differences of orthogonal linear-analyzer intensities on axes separated by 45 degrees, and S3 as a convention-specified circular-intensity difference.
Stokes parameters can represent partially polarized or unpolarized light; nonzero total intensity does not require nonzero polarization components.
accepted_variants: I,Q,U,V denote total intensity, horizontal-minus-vertical, plus-45-minus-minus-45, and a declared right-minus-left circular difference; reversing the last sign convention is acceptable if consistent.
major_error_concepts: Calling a nonzero (S0,0,0,0) vector zero light or fully polarized.
Claiming Stokes parameters require a single deterministic Jones vector for every beam.
Using a circular-polarization sign as universal without specifying handedness convention.

cards.prompt: What is Unpolarized Light? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Unpolarized light has no preferred polarization direction in the relevant statistical description, while partially polarized light contains both polarized and unpolarized contributions. These statements concern averages, not absence of an instantaneous electromagnetic field.
required_concepts: Statistical polarization mixture rather than zero field.
major_error_concepts: Calling unpolarized light an electromagnetic wave with no electric-field direction at any instant.

cards.prompt: What is Linear Polarizer? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: An ideal linear polarizer transmits one transverse electric-field component and rejects the orthogonal one. For unpolarized input, its transmitted intensity is half the incident intensity in the ideal lossless-pass-axis model.
required_concepts: Projection onto one polarization axis.
Half intensity for ideal unpolarized input.
major_error_concepts: Assuming an ideal polarizer transmits half of every already polarized input regardless of angle.

cards.prompt: What is Malus Law? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Malus's law gives transmitted intensity I=I_0 cos squared theta for linearly polarized light passing through an ideal analyzer at angle theta to its polarization axis. It is an intensity law arising from projecting field amplitude.
required_concepts: Cosine-squared intensity dependence for polarized input.
major_error_concepts: Using cosine rather than cosine squared for transmitted intensity.

cards.prompt: What is Birefringence? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Birefringence means distinct polarization eigenstates experience different phase indices in a material for the specified propagation direction. It can split rays or accumulate a relative phase, depending on geometry and propagation.
required_concepts: Polarization-dependent refractive indices.
major_error_concepts: Assuming a birefringent material must give the same phase velocity to all polarizations in every direction.

cards.prompt: What is Crystal Optic Axis? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: An optic axis in a uniaxial crystal is a direction along which the ordinary and extraordinary phase indices coincide in the ideal description. It is a material symmetry direction, not simply the arbitrary laboratory beam axis.
required_concepts: Special crystal direction with coincident phase indices in the uniaxial model.
major_error_concepts: Equating a crystal optic axis with any chosen apparatus optical axis regardless of crystal orientation.

cards.prompt: What is Optical Retardance? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A wave plate introduces a relative phase delay between orthogonal polarization eigencomponents through different optical path lengths. For a uniform simple plate, retardance is 2pi Delta n L/lambda_vacuum modulo two pi, with axis and sign conventions stated.
required_concepts: Relative eigenpolarization phase from index difference and thickness.
major_error_concepts: Assuming a wave plate changes only intensity while leaving relative phase unchanged.

cards.prompt: What is Quarter-Wave Plate? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: An ideal quarter-wave plate introduces a relative phase of pi/2 modulo the relevant full-wave convention. It converts linear light to circular only when the incident field has equal amplitudes along its two eigenaxes with suitable alignment.
required_concepts: Quarter-cycle relative delay.
Circular output requires equal axis components.
major_error_concepts: Claiming every linear input angle becomes circular after a quarter-wave plate.

cards.prompt: What is Half-Wave Plate? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: An ideal half-wave plate introduces a relative phase of pi between eigencomponents. For linear input it rotates the polarization orientation by twice the angle between the input direction and the chosen plate axis, interpreted modulo the axis convention.
required_concepts: Half-cycle delay and twice-angle linear polarization transformation.
major_error_concepts: Assuming a half-wave plate necessarily depolarizes a fully polarized input.

cards.prompt: What is Brewster Angle? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: At Brewster incidence for a simple transparent nonmagnetic isotropic interface, the reflected p-polarized amplitude vanishes and tan theta_B=n_2/n_1. The angle is measured from the normal; absorption or more general media can change the result.
required_concepts: Zero p reflection under stated ideal dielectric assumptions.
major_error_concepts: Claiming all polarization components vanish in reflection at the Brewster angle.

cards.prompt: What is Fresnel Coefficients? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Fresnel coefficients give reflected and transmitted field amplitudes for specified incident polarization and interface conditions. Converting them to power fractions requires the appropriate index, angle, and impedance factors, so field amplitude and energy coefficients are distinct.
required_concepts: Polarization-specific interface field ratios.
Power conversion requires geometric and material factors.
major_error_concepts: Treating a transmitted electric-field amplitude ratio squared as the power ratio in every unequal-medium geometry without correction.

cards.prompt: What is Antireflection Coating? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: An antireflection coating uses chosen layer indices and optical thicknesses to cancel reflected amplitudes over a design range. Performance depends on wavelength, incidence angle, polarization, and layer design rather than one universal cancellation for all light.
required_concepts: Thin-layer interference reduces selected reflected amplitudes.
major_error_concepts: Claiming one quarter-wave layer eliminates reflection at every wavelength and incidence angle.

cards.prompt: What is Optical Absorption? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Optical absorption transfers electromagnetic energy into material excitations or other internal energy channels. It differs from purely elastic redirection by scattering and is represented by a lossy material response in wave models.
required_concepts: Optical energy transfer into material channels.
major_error_concepts: Calling all missing forward-beam intensity absorption even when light is merely scattered out of the detector aperture.

cards.prompt: What is Beer-Lambert Law? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: For uniform linear attenuation with constant intensity coefficient alpha, a collimated beam follows I(L)=I_0 exp(-alpha L) when the model's loss and geometry assumptions hold. Absorption, scattering, saturation, and reflections must be separated according to what alpha represents.
required_concepts: Exponential intensity attenuation with stated coefficient meaning.
major_error_concepts: Applying a linear exponential law unchanged in a saturating or multiply scattering regime without justification.

cards.prompt: What is Optical Scattering? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Optical scattering redistributes incident light into other directions through interaction with particles or spatial variations. Scattered power may leave a detector's acceptance without being absorbed, and the angular pattern depends on size, wavelength, and material response.
required_concepts: Directional redistribution distinct from absorption.
major_error_concepts: Assuming scattering must destroy photon energy rather than redirecting it in the elastic case.

cards.prompt: What is Laser? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A laser combines optical gain from stimulated emission with feedback or another suitable amplification arrangement to produce selected optical modes. Laser light often has high coherence, but bandwidth, mode structure, and noise vary across lasers.
required_concepts: Stimulated gain with mode-selective feedback or amplification.
major_error_concepts: Assuming every laser emits one perfectly monochromatic noiseless mode.

cards.prompt: What is Stimulated Emission? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Stimulated emission occurs when an incident optical field induces an excited system to emit into the stimulating mode under the relevant transition conditions. It differs from spontaneous emission, whose mode and phase are not set by the same incoming coherent drive.
required_concepts: Field-induced emission into the stimulating mode.
major_error_concepts: Equating stimulated emission with absorption of the incoming photon without an emitted field contribution.

cards.prompt: What is Laser Resonator? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A laser resonator selects frequencies and spatial patterns through round-trip phase and feedback conditions. Oscillation threshold requires small-signal round-trip gain to balance losses; above threshold gain saturation influences steady operation.
required_concepts: Cavity mode selection and gain-loss threshold.
major_error_concepts: Assuming adding mirrors alone creates laser oscillation without a gain source exceeding losses.

cards.prompt: What is Gaussian Beam? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A fundamental Gaussian beam is a paraxial wave solution with a Gaussian transverse field profile and a finite waist. It diffracts as it propagates, so an ideal finite-width Gaussian beam is not an exactly nonspreading cylinder.
required_concepts: Gaussian transverse paraxial mode with diffraction.
major_error_concepts: Assuming a finite Gaussian beam stays at one fixed radius for arbitrary propagation distance.

cards.prompt: What is Beam Waist? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: The Gaussian beam waist is the plane of minimum beam radius under the chosen amplitude or intensity-radius convention. In the common convention w is the radius at which intensity falls to exp(-2) of its on-axis value.
required_concepts: Minimum beam radius with explicit radius convention.
major_error_concepts: Mixing a half-maximum intensity radius with the usual exp(-2) radius without conversion.

cards.prompt: What is Rayleigh Range? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: For an ideal Gaussian beam in vacuum, the Rayleigh range is z_R=pi w_0 squared/lambda. At distance z_R from the waist, the standard radius is sqrt(2) times w_0, marking the scale of diffraction spreading.
required_concepts: Rayleigh range pi w_0 squared/lambda in vacuum.
Radius grows by sqrt(2) at that distance.
major_error_concepts: Calling z_R the distance where beam radius doubles rather than grows by sqrt(2).

cards.prompt: What is Gaussian Beam Divergence? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: An ideal Gaussian beam in vacuum has far-field divergence half-angle approximately lambda/(pi w_0) in the paraxial convention. A smaller waist therefore requires larger angular spread, and real-beam quality can broaden the product.
required_concepts: Waist-divergence inverse tradeoff with half-angle convention.
major_error_concepts: Claiming an arbitrarily small waist can retain arbitrarily small divergence at fixed wavelength.

cards.prompt: What is Etendue? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Optical etendue describes the phase-space extent of a ray bundle through area and solid angle with refractive-index weighting. In ideal passive lossless geometrical optics it is conserved, constraining how much extended-source light can be concentrated.
required_concepts: Index-weighted area-angular extent.
Concentration constrained by conservation.
major_error_concepts: Assuming all extended-source rays can be compressed to arbitrarily small area and angle simultaneously by passive optics.

cards.prompt: What is Optical Detection? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: An optical detector converts incident radiation into a measurable signal with finite spectral response, efficiency, bandwidth, and noise. A measured electrical signal requires calibration to infer optical power and does not directly equal field amplitude in every detector.
required_concepts: Radiation-to-signal conversion with response and calibration.
major_error_concepts: Assuming identical detector outputs at all wavelengths correspond to identical incident power without response calibration.

cards.prompt: What is Photon Shot Noise? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: In an ideal independent photon-counting model, shot noise has count standard deviation equal to the square root of the mean count. Background, detector noise, and non-Poisson light can change the observed statistics, so the model must be identified.
required_concepts: Poisson count variance equals mean under independent counting assumptions.
major_error_concepts: Claiming every optical noise process has Poisson variance regardless of source statistics or detector contributions.

cards.prompt: What is Optical Sampling? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Digital optical sampling records an image or signal at finite spatial or temporal intervals. Sampling too coarsely can alias variations beyond the permitted band, and more pixels do not recover detail already removed by the optical transfer function.
required_concepts: Finite sampling can alias high-frequency content.
Sampling cannot undo absent optical information automatically.
major_error_concepts: Assuming arbitrarily many detector pixels guarantee unlimited optical resolution through a fixed finite aperture.

description: A definition-recall course deck covering core concepts in Optics.
